title_original: Hassan Hajjaj, the Eye That Grooves
excerpt_original: The British-Moroccan photographer Hassan Hajjaj takes over the Philharmonie de Paris with some forty portraits turned up loud: rock stars all his own, from Madonna to the Malian duo Amadou & Mariam. L’article Hassan Hajjaj, the Eye That Grooves est apparu en premier sur Blind…

blocks.text: The session with Amadou & Mariam stays among his favorites. A devotee of the Bamako duo, Hassan Hajjaj built them a playlist of Gnawa and Brazilian capoeira, something earthy enough to hold in your hands; when the shoot wound down, the musicians were the ones asking him for the tracklist. He has always worked like this: lens in hand, music in the ear.

Born in 1961 in Larache, a fishing town on Morocco’s northwest coast, he grows up among photographers of every stripe. On the street and the sand, the picture is taken, a paper slip changes hands, and the print turns up a few days later. In the studio, stool and backdrop at the ready, he comes with the family in their Sunday best to sit for the portrait posted, every two years, to the father who has left to work in London. The boy follows in 1973, at thirteen, straight into the racial tensions of the late 1970s, somewhere between the Jamaican sound systems and Rock Against Racism.

“Music creates bonds and connections,” sums up Inès Geoffroy, the exhibition’s curator; for this uprooted boy it will be a shared tongue, and already a weapon. In 1984, Hassan Hajjaj opens Real Artistic People on Neal Street, Covent Garden: a do-it-yourself clothing shop (creative make-do, part handmade craft, part militant recycling) with a basement of vinyl to rummage through. He prints “Chanel No. 5 for Gucci” on T-shirts, splices Vivienne Westwood into New York hip-hop, stitches spoof labels onto the backs of denim jackets.

The shop turns into a den for musicians, painters, photographers and poets, what Hassan Hajjaj will later call his “university.” Fab 5 Freddy, the cult host of Yo! MTV Raps , pushes through the door one day and reads his project on sight: “the Moroccan, Arab, Muslim side of hip-hop fashion and street style,” the artist recalled to Blind. The way he shoots comes from the same place. He dresses his subjects himself: djellabas in geometric print, babouches trimmed with hijacked logos, kaftans the color of sour sweets, veils in polka dots or counterfeit luxury crests, the whole thing staged against backdrops of woven, multicolored plastic.

“He really had this approach, a bit like making a great mix: sampling, collecting motifs, formats, colors,” Inès Geoffroy observes, “a world where design and music stand on the same level.” The Malian masters Seydou Keïta and Malick Sidibé, who invented the modern African studio portrait, preside over every frame; Hassan Hajjaj claims them as forefathers, then tilts their legacy toward a language all his own: hybrid, festive, gloriously cobbled together.

The photographer helps himself to the European cliché of the rock star, leather jacket, Ray-Bans, electric guitar, and hands the crown to his own instead. Madonna makes the case: shot in Marrakech for her sixtieth birthday, she sits in babouches sewn from rice sacks, a mock-Gucci print, a would-be Louis Vuitton hat, every piece made by Hassan Hajjaj. Veiled, hidden behind her shades, she turns unrecognizable, then leaves for the airport without changing a thing.

Lee Scratch Perry, the high priest of Jamaican dub, turns up as a silent watcher on set. The photographer slides a pair of plastic shoes his way; the musician pulls them on at once and, that same night, takes the stage in the full getup. Others file past the lens too: Keziah Jones, Cardi B, then Alicia Keys and her husband, the producer Swizz Beatz, who collect his work. The show’s poster goes to Billie Eilish: in 2019, on a Vogue shoot in Los Angeles, Hassan Hajjaj talks the singer, barely eighteen and chaperoned by her mother, into his own designs. “I’ve met so many incredible people, who are my real rock stars,” he told Blind, “what they do, they have it in their blood.”

blocks.text: The frames he builds himself, worked like sculpture. “What really makes the signature is framing the photos with tin cans, salvaged or made by his own hand,” notes Marion Challier, curator; “Hassan Hajjaj is deeply attached to salvage as a way of life.” Harissa, tomato, green tea, their logos curling into Arabic, run around the edge of every portrait. Each print is dated twice over, Gregorian and Hijri: a quiet reminder that time itself keeps different counts from one shore to the next.

At the Philharmonie as in his life, Gnawa runs through everything. After twelve years of London’s electronic nights, hungry for something to feed the soul, Hassan Hajjaj goes back to the sound of this brotherhood of healer-musicians, in Marrakech, in the early 1990s. The exhibition’s own soundtrack may come from Acid Arab, electronica braided into Arab tradition over a bed of acid house, yet it is two Gnawa masters, Ba Bohot and Khadija Lgnawia, who hold pride of place. A tribute to a culture from which he drew, he confides, “something that touched my spirit, my heart, my frequencies.”
“Hassan Hajjaj, My Rock Stars” is on view at the Musée de la musique – Philharmonie de Paris through April 25, 2027.
